title: The Mechanics of Pre-suasion: Causes, Constraints, and Correctives
hook: The first screen on the triage tablet can ready shame before symptoms are even sorted.
counterintuition: Prepared concepts are not commands. They are temporary activations that help or distort depending on relevance, limits, and the corrective you place nearby.
tryThisNow: Find one first cue in a form or script. Write what it readies, what it could distort, and the correction that should appear before the decision.
keyTakeaway: Pre-suasion works by readying concepts, so check the cause and the boundary before trusting any opening cue.

breakdown.fastRead:
A triage tablet pauses on insurance before symptoms. Patients answer pain questions differently after thinking about coverage. The nurse manager moves the insurance screen later and compares the responses. The prepared concept changed the next answer.

This is the mechanics level. A cue readies a concept, and a readied concept is easier to activate when the next information arrives. The cue still has limits. If it distorts the wrong answer, the sequence needs a corrective.
breakdown.deepRead:
A court administrator reorders a jury questionnaire. Neighborhood questions once appeared before evidence instructions, and later fairness ratings shifted around assumptions the form never meant to raise. She moves those questions after the instruction sheet and tracks what changes.

Readied is not the same as controlled.

The source support makes a careful claim: pre-suasion focuses recipients first on concepts associatively aligned with information still to come. Mental elements fire not only when ready, but when readied. That explains the effect without turning it into mystery or permanent programming.

A loan script shows the constraint. If the opening recites balance due, callers may hear hardship options through shame. A neutral identity check before the option sheet can reduce that spillover. The corrective is not cosmetic. It changes which concept is active when help is offered.
breakdown.fullRead:
A glowing answer button under a science-museum question panel can ready curiosity. That is useful if the next label honors uncertainty. It is misleading if the exhibit makes a guess feel like a fact. The designer adds a correction label beside the mystery prompt before visitors press the answer button: what we know, what we are still testing.

Mechanics keep the practice honest. A cue has a cause: it makes some concept easier to activate. A cue has constraints: the effect is temporary, context-bound, and vulnerable to mismatch. A cue needs correctives when it might spread beyond the decision it should inform.

Look at the restaurant menu owner testing health icons. A red icon beside a balanced dish may ready caution so strongly that diners avoid the dish for the wrong reason. The sales tally does not prove the icon is bad. It asks whether the cue’s reach exceeded its job.

What did the first cue make easier to think, and where should that ease stop?

An HR analyst sees the word complaint at the top of a feedback survey and worries it will ready resentment across every answer. She removes it from the opener and adds a later corrective item that asks for one working practice to preserve. The survey still collects problems. It no longer primes the whole form as grievance.

The clean use of mechanics is humble. You do not plant any idea and make it work. You ready one relevant concept, watch for spillover, and build a correction where fairness requires it.

examples.title: Erin Moves Insurance After Symptoms

planSpec.audience: a nurse manager checking whether a pain-scale prompt readies the wrong concern
planSpec.stakes: whether a prepared concept helps or distorts the next answer
planSpec.requiredBeat: the manager compares responses when insurance questions come before versus after symptom sorting

examples.scenario: A triage tablet pauses on the insurance screen while Erin lays a symptom card beside it. In the postmortem, she compares pain-scale responses from days when coverage questions came first with days when symptoms came first. The answers shift. Erin is not inventing a protocol; she is deciding whether the first screen readied money worries before patients described pain.
examples.whatToDo: Move insurance questions after symptom sorting and compare response patterns. Keep the coverage screen from readying the wrong concern.
examples.whyItMatters: A first concept can color the next answer. The sequence matters when money anxiety may distort clinical description.

examples.title: Victoria Reorders the Neighborhood Tabs

planSpec.audience: a court administrator testing whether early questions bias later fairness ratings
planSpec.stakes: whether readied concepts can be corrected by order changes
planSpec.requiredBeat: the administrator moves neighborhood questions after evidence instructions and tracks what changes

examples.scenario: A questionnaire packet with reordered tabs sits beside an instruction sheet as Victoria reviews juror forms. At 1:10 p.m. in the courthouse form room, Victoria is the court administrator deciding which question order will be tested before summons packets print. Neighborhood questions used to appear before fairness ratings. She must decide before printing whether to keep the old order or move those tabs after the evidence instructions and track changes. The new order tests whether a readied place concept was leaking into judgments it should not touch.
examples.whatToDo: Move neighborhood questions after evidence instructions and compare fairness ratings. Use order as a corrective, not as a hidden lever.
examples.whyItMatters: The place concept may be relevant later, but early activation can spill into fairness ratings before evidence rules are clear.

examples.title: Monica Strikes the Balance Line First

planSpec.audience: a bank compliance officer limiting priming by debt language
planSpec.stakes: whether callers are readied for shame before hearing options
planSpec.requiredBeat: the officer replaces the opening balance recitation with a neutral identity check and compares take-up

examples.scenario: A call script lies on Monica’s desk with the balance line struck through and a hardship option sheet underneath. Before the edit, callers heard the amount due first and often declined help. After the edit, the opening is a neutral identity check, then options. Monica compares take-up and listens for shame in the call notes. She is deciding whether the old first sentence readied the wrong self.
examples.whatToDo: Replace the opening balance recitation with a neutral identity check, then present hardship options clearly.
examples.whyItMatters: Debt language can ready shame before help appears. The correction lets callers hear options before the balance defines the conversation.

examples.title: Jonas Adds the Uncertainty Label

planSpec.audience: an exhibit designer showing uncertainty without making guesses feel like facts
planSpec.stakes: whether readied curiosity stays inside evidence limits
planSpec.requiredBeat: the designer adds a correction label beside the mystery prompt before visitors press the answer button

examples.scenario: An exhibit button glows under a question panel while Jonas holds a correction label. At 2:45 p.m. on the museum floor, Jonas is the exhibit lead deciding how to keep the correction visible before visitors press the answer button. Visitors are about to decide whether the mystery answer is settled fact. Before the answer button opens, he adds a label that says what is known and what remains under test. Curiosity still pulls them in, but the correction sits beside the cue before the guess hardens.
examples.whatToDo: Place the correction label beside the mystery prompt before visitors press the answer button. Let curiosity meet its evidence limits immediately.
examples.whyItMatters: Mystery readies belief in an answer. The correction keeps curiosity from turning a provisional explanation into certainty.

examples.title: Greta Tests the Red Icon’s Reach

planSpec.audience: a menu owner testing if health icons crowd out taste decisions too strongly
planSpec.stakes: whether a cue’s reach exceeds the decision it should inform
planSpec.requiredBeat: the owner checks whether diners avoid balanced dishes with one red icon before changing the icon system

examples.scenario: A menu proof shows red icons beside three entrees while Greta compares the sales tally. At 11:30 a.m. in the cafe office, Greta is the menu owner deciding whether the red icon makes diners think health or danger. In the postmortem, one balanced dish with a single red icon fell harder than richer dishes without icons. She checks whether diners avoided it as unhealthy before changing the system. The cue was meant to inform, not make one mark define the whole plate.
examples.whatToDo: Compare sales by icon pattern before redesigning the menu. Keep health cues from reaching beyond the specific information they carry.
examples.whyItMatters: A red icon can ready caution so strongly that taste and balance disappear. The tally tests whether the cue exceeded its useful limit.

examples.title: Henrik Removes Complaint From the Opener

planSpec.audience: an HR analyst preventing one word from contaminating all answers
planSpec.stakes: whether readied resentment spreads beyond the target issue
planSpec.requiredBeat: the analyst removes the word complaint from the opener and adds a later corrective item

examples.scenario: A survey preview shows the first prompt highlighted while Henrik studies a response heatmap from last quarter. The word complaint sat in the opener and seemed to pull resentment through unrelated answers. He removes it and adds a later corrective item asking what should be preserved. The survey still invites problems, but the first concept no longer contaminates the whole form.
examples.whatToDo: Remove complaint from the opener and add a later preserve item. Let criticism appear where it belongs without readying resentment everywhere.
examples.whyItMatters: One early word can activate a frame across the survey. The corrective restores range so every answer is not pulled toward grievance.

questions.prompt: A triage form asks insurance questions before symptom sorting, and pain answers change. What is the likely mechanism? At triage intake, the nurse manager must decide whether the first screen readies money worries before symptom answers.
choices: Insurance questions are always irrelevant in emergency rooms.
Coverage concerns may be readied before patients describe symptoms.
Pain answers are too subjective to use.
questions.explanation: The order may activate money anxiety before pain reporting. The point is not that coverage never matters, but that early activation can distort the next answer.

questions.prompt: A jury questionnaire asks neighborhood questions before fairness ratings. What corrective best tests spillover? Before the jury form is printed, the administrator must decide how to test whether neighborhood questions are spilling into fairness ratings.
choices: Delete every neighborhood question.
Move those questions after evidence instructions and track rating changes.
Tell jurors not to be biased.
questions.explanation: Reordering tests whether the early concept was contaminating fairness ratings. Deletion may lose useful information, and a warning alone may not change activation.

questions.prompt: A hardship call opens with the balance due, and callers decline options. What should the compliance officer try? During a compliance review of the call script, the officer must decide whether balance-first wording readies shame before help appears.
choices: Repeat the balance more slowly so callers understand it.
Hide the balance until after enrollment.
Open with a neutral identity check, then present the option sheet.
questions.explanation: A neutral opener reduces shame activation before help appears. Repeating the balance may deepen the problem, while hiding it removes relevant information.

questions.prompt: A museum mystery prompt makes visitors treat a guess as settled fact. Which correction fits? On the museum floor, the exhibit lead must decide how to keep curiosity open without letting the first guess become false certainty.
choices: Remove all curiosity from the exhibit.
Make the answer button larger.
Add a label beside the prompt showing what is known and what remains under test.
questions.explanation: The correction keeps curiosity inside evidence limits. Removing curiosity wastes a useful magnetizer, and a larger button would intensify the same problem.

questions.prompt: A red nutrition icon makes diners avoid a balanced dish. What should the menu owner ask? Before the menu goes to print, the owner must decide whether the red icon readies health or warning in the wrong place.
choices: Whether diners are too emotional to read menus.
Whether the icon’s caution cue exceeded the exact information it should carry.
Whether all nutrition information should be hidden.
questions.explanation: The issue is cue reach. The icon may ready caution beyond its intended scope; insulting diners or hiding all information misses the corrective test.

questions.prompt: A survey opener uses the word complaint, and unrelated answers become harsher. What revision is strongest? In a survey preview, the analyst must decide whether the first word readies complaint mode before unrelated questions begin.
choices: Add a cheerful image above the complaint prompt.
Keep the opener and tell employees to be balanced.
Use a neutral opener and add a later item asking what should be preserved.
questions.explanation: The neutral opener prevents broad resentment activation, and the preserve item corrects range. Cheerful images and instructions do not address the readied concept.

questions.prompt: Someone says priming can plant any idea and make people act. What is the best reply?
choices: Readied concepts can influence what comes next, but relevance, timing, and correctives limit the effect.
Priming is fake because people always decide consciously.
Priming works forever once the cue appears.
questions.explanation: The answer keeps the mechanism and the limits together. The other choices deny the effect or exaggerate it into permanent control.

questions.prompt: A form opens with “fraud warning” before asking users to rate ordinary service quality. Ratings fall sharply. What should be evaluated?
choices: Whether users dislike warnings in general.
Whether fraud language readied suspicion that spilled into unrelated ratings.
Whether all service ratings are unreliable.
questions.explanation: The early warning may activate suspicion beyond its proper target. The corrective is to test placement and scope, not dismiss ratings altogether.

questions.prompt: A designer wants to use a curiosity cue before a medical-risk explanation. Which plan is most responsible?
choices: Open a question the explanation answers, and place uncertainty limits next to the cue.
Open with the most frightening mystery possible.
Withhold the answer until users agree to the recommendation.
questions.explanation: The responsible plan pairs activation with an immediate corrective. Fear and withholding both exploit the opened loop rather than helping people judge.

reviewCards.front: What does it mean for a concept to be readied?
reviewCards.back: A cue has made the concept easier to activate when the next information arrives. It is influence, not control.

reviewCards.front: A form asks money questions before pain questions. What should you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: The early cue may ready money anxiety and distort symptom reporting. Move it later and compare responses.

reviewCards.front: What are the three checks on a prepared concept?
reviewCards.back: Cause, constraint, and corrective: what it readies, where the effect should stop, and what prevents spillover.

reviewCards.front: Why add an uncertainty label beside a mystery prompt?
reviewCards.back: Curiosity readies belief in an answer. The label keeps visitors inside the evidence rather than letting mystery harden into certainty.

reviewCards.front: A survey starts with complaint and everything sounds harsher. What is the fix?
reviewCards.back: Use a neutral opener and add a later corrective item that asks what should be preserved, so criticism does not swallow the whole form.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The skill is auditing the first cue for activation and spillover. You ask what concept the cue readies, whether that concept belongs, and what correction keeps judgment fair.

ifThenPlans.plan: If an early form question may ready shame or suspicion, then move it after neutral sorting and compare responses.
If a call opens with debt language, then test a neutral identity check before presenting help.
If curiosity is used, then place the evidence limit beside the question before the answer appears.
If one word may contaminate every answer, then replace it in the opener and add a later balancing item.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Find the first cue in one form, script, or meeting. Write three lines: readies, distorts, corrects. Change the cue if the corrective is missing.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, audit a sequence of questions or screens. Move one cue later, add one corrective, and record whether the answers become cleaner.

memorableLines.text: Readied is not the same as controlled.
memorableLines.why: It keeps the mechanism bounded and credible.
It frames the chapter as disciplined testing rather than mystique.

memorableLines.text: You ready one relevant concept, watch for spillover, and build a correction where fairness requires it.
memorableLines.why: It summarizes cause, constraint, and corrective in one actionable line.
